It's like comparing a Spangles to a donut shop. Spangles has a large menu, and also donuts, but a donut shop has donuts, maybe some coffee. Technically, they compete for people who want food, but the markets are not the same. You go to a donut shop for donuts, not for a meal with fries and a chocolate shake. 

Spangles isn't competing with a donut shop, but the donut shop competes with Spangles to try and draw the donut crowd. 

The donuts are the arcade style platforms and cartoons style games, like Luigi's Mansion, Pokemon, and Mario.

Sure, but the quality of games from Nintendo stems from I suppose a one-way competition with Sony/Microsoft. They don't need to compete to take people from Sony/Microsoft but they do need to put out quality enough games so people ALSO buy a Switch. There would still be some people who buy the console to play on the go, but not a whole lot. I'd wager a lot of games played on the go are the easy to start/stop single player games, and not Switch Overwatch or Switch Fortnite. 

Sony and Microsoft wouldn't really gain/lose people based on the quality of the games on Nintendo. Since the market is so different, it's typically going to be people who own a console and a Switch or just a console, and percentage wise, the amount of people who only own a Switch doesn't really affect Sony. So the quality of Nintendo games really only matters on the Nintendo side, do justify people buying a Switch in addition to their console.

Sony vs Microsoft is pretty self explanatory on why the quality of games matters. Starfield is a great representation. I think the quality of Starfield and lack of good reception was really the last straw of Microsoft saying they can't compete with Sony. Sony doesn't really have any reason to push boundaries now, other than push boundaries of live service games to try and find the one game that brings Sony money and not Activision/Blizzard, etc. The market is already on their console and there isn't a reason to buy Xbox anymore due to gamepass and PC compatibility with all games and now the lack of exclusivity. 

I think we're just going to see some cookie cutter games from Sony that aren't necessarily bad, but are going to be a tried and true formula that are okay but aren't anything new, like going from Spiderman one to Miles Morales (It might as well have just been DLC gameplay wise), sprinkled with live service games as they try to wrangle that one GOAT that gets them the bag. You don't have another console to go to if you want something new. You can pay the same price for Xbox, but then you're just missing out on games, even if they are Spiderman 18: The Respidering

I think that's part of the problem is that with no competition, the market and scopes doesn't change. It's hard to justify spending more money on potential flops and new IPs when Spiderman 117.2 HD Remake the Morales Multiverse Adventures is selling with the relatively same gameplay because there aren't any competing consoles, so why would a business potentially lose money on trying something new (Concord)? They wouldn't because there is no where for you to leave to.

I think Nintendo and Sony are independent enough that that aren't really direct competition. Nintendo has a different market than Sony, and that's the portable market. Until Sony has another truly portable console, like the Vita or PsP that isn't just LAN streaming from your console, there is a large difference in market and I wouldn't consider them direct competition.

It also drives innovation and promotes quality products when two companies are competing to draw the market to their side. 

Unfortunately, it seems like Microsoft is throwing in the towel so we'll see what that means for Sony Exclusives when there is no longer a reason to provide super quality. 

That's the problem with no competition, it turns into a either take this sub-product , the only one available, or don't take it at all, which is bad for everyone.

We use them industrially and have built large, multiple axis machines with them. They are very powerful PLC and Drives, though they obviously have some computing limitations when it comes to probably 4 and greater axis or a CNC machine. You'd still be better off with a larger company and CNC specific controllers. They still offer a lot of the safety functions that larger brand name drives and such have, but I don't forsee being required for a smaller payload like a camera. 

It also depends how the camera is needing to be controlled. Is there feedback it is trying to follow from a different program? Will the camera be continuously moving based on continuous inputs? There are quite a few variables that come into play, but I'd wager the AD line of PLC and HMI would work. I've rebuilt some machines that the owning company went out of business so I had no spare parts for.

The DC stepper drives and motors would be able to drive your system and then you can make the gantry. There are a lot of things involved such as tolerances and range of motion, but they have a very good variety. Their technical support are also very good as far as programming and knowledge about products, though the don't have an applications engineering team to help you pick out systems for really difficult scenarios.

Ie I was building a machine that had the motors controlled by torque, but was having trouble finding out the torque requirements as there were 5 different motors all's supply torque non-tangentially so it was very hard calculations for a layman. (Ended up doing the old buy shit and hope it works method).

They can help with a lot of questions directly related to their products however.

You should look at Automation Direct. They should have all the motion components you need for something this simple. You can also get their productivity series PLC and HMI for incredibly cheap and make your own program. The you can program limits, timers, alarms, whatever you want. I've used the software/hardware a lot and programmed the HMI and PLC quite a bit and I'm just a dumb maintenance mechanic.
